record.paper_title: On the combinatorics of tableaux -- A notebook of open problems
record.original_question: Prove that a locally-finite distributive lattice has a lattice of ideals of prime filters that contains at most three connected components (one isomorphic to the lattice, perhaps one containing the empty ideal, and perhaps one containing the ideal of all primes) iff the lattice has finite width (contains no infinite antichains).

evidence.quote: [Wor2026c] Prove that a locally-finite distributive lattice has a lattice of ideals of prime filters that contains at most three connected components (one isomorphic to the lattice, perhaps one containing the empty ideal, and perhaps one containing the ideal of all primes) iff the lattice has finite width (contains no infinite antichains).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $L$ be a locally-finite distributive lattice, i.e., a distributive lattice in which every finitely generated sublattice is finite. A filter of $L$ is a nonempty upward-closed subset $F \subseteq L$ that is closed under finite meets. A filter $F$ is called prime if its complement $L \setminus F$ is closed under finite joins (equivalently, $x \vee y \in F$ implies $x \in F$ or $y \in F$). Let $\mathrm{Spec}(L)$ denote the collection of all prime filters of $L$. An ideal of $\mathrm{Spec}(L)$ is a subset $I \subseteq \mathrm{Spec}(L)$ that is downward-closed under inclusion (i.e., if $P \in I$ and $Q \subseteq P$ is a prime filter, then $Q \in I$). Order the set $\mathcal{I}$ of all such ideals by inclusion; this is itself a lattice. Define a graph on $\mathcal{I}$ whose edges connect ideals that differ by the addition or removal of a single prime filter, and let the connected components of $\mathcal{I}$ be the connected components of this graph (equivalently, the components in the covering graph of the ideal lattice).

The width of $L$ is the supremum of the cardinalities of antichains in $L$; $L$ is said to have finite width if it contains no infinite antichain.

Prove or disprove: $\mathcal{I}$ has at most three connected components — one component naturally isomorphic to $L$ itself, possibly one component containing the empty ideal, and possibly one component containing the ideal consisting of all prime filters of $L$ — if and only if $L$ has finite width.
